title: Light Maps and Uniformity Metrics
objective: Create spatial light maps and report distribution with metrics that do not hide crop-relevant dark zones or hotspots.

terms.definition: Defined set of measurement coordinates over a crop area.
A declared comparison such as minimum divided by mean; the exact formula must be stated.
Standard deviation divided by mean, usually expressed as a percentage.
Estimate between measured points; an analytical aid that does not replace adequate sampling.

coreScience: A light map preserves location. Use a fixed coordinate system, consistent cell size, and a crop-relevant measurement plane. Include edges, corners, fixture seams, and known obstructions; a grid that samples only expected good areas is biased.

Mean PPFD alone can conceal a crop with damaging hotspots and unproductive lows. Report the raw grid plus minimum, maximum, median, mean, standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and a clearly defined uniformity ratio. Percentiles can be more stable than a single extreme when measurement density is high, but extremes still require investigation.

Comparisons require identical geometry and operating conditions. Mapping an empty room may commission the installation, while mapping a mature canopy evaluates a different optical system because leaves absorb, reflect, and redistribute photons. Version each map with fixture layout and canopy state.
cultivationRelevance: Distribution often controls consistency more than the headline average. It affects morphology, transpiration, maturation, quality grading, irrigation demand, and risk of localized high-light stress.
Maps support fixture spacing, dimming zones, crop placement, maintenance, and acceptance testing after changes.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Room, bench, date, crop stage, fixture layout revision, and operator.
Origin, spacing, dimensions, measurement plane, coordinate labels, and excluded areas.
Dimming, channels, warm-up, curtains, wall reflectance condition, and sunlight status.
Raw values, mean, median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation, CV, and stated uniformity formula.
Hotspot or low-zone investigation, adjustment, remap date, and crop-response verification.

misconceptions: Average PPFD proves uniformity: Different distributions can have the same mean.
Minimum divided by maximum is the universal metric: Multiple definitions are used; the formula and sampling scheme must accompany the number.
A heat map proves unsampled values: Interpolation can create visual certainty that the measurement grid does not support.
evidenceLimits: Uniformity acceptance criteria depend on crop architecture, economics, fixture system, measurement density, and the consequence of local extremes. No single threshold is universal.
